# Tailored ISO 27001 Gap Analysis

---

## 1. Prioritized Gap-Analysis Checklist

### 🔴 HIGH PRIORITY — Do first (certification blockers)

These are either mandatory clauses or high-risk gaps given your healthcare/telehealth context.

**ISMS Foundation (Clauses 4–6, 9–10)**

| Gap | What to produce / evidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| No formal ISMS scope statement | Documented scope covering clinic, telehealth, Azure, SaaS EHR, on-prem, MSSP relationship | Clause 4.3 — auditor checks this first |
| No information security policy suite | Overarching ISMS policy signed by top management, plus topic-specific policies | Clause 5.2 — your AUP and BYOD are a start, not sufficient |
| No formal risk assessment process | Risk assessment methodology, risk register, risk treatment plan | Clause 6.1.2 — the heart of the audit |
| No Statement of Applicability (SoA) | SoA listing all 93 Annex A controls with justification for inclusion/exclusion | Clause 6.1.3(d) — mandatory document |
| No management review records | Scheduled management review meetings with minutes | Clause 9.3 — at least annual |
| No internal audit programme | Internal audit plan, audit reports, corrective actions | Clause 9.2 — must exist before Stage 2 |

**Critical Annex A Gaps**

| Ref | Control area | Gap in your org | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.9 | Asset inventory | CMDB incomplete — you can't protect what you don't know | Complete asset register: hardware, software, data assets, cloud services, owners assigned |
| 5.10–5.12 | Acceptable use, return, classification | AUP exists but no data classification scheme | Classification policy (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), handling rules — vital for PHI |
| 8.8 | Vulnerability management | Irregular scanning | Documented VM policy with defined scan cadence, SLAs for remediation by severity, evidence of remediation |
| 5.19–5.22 | Supplier security | MSSP and SaaS EHR are critical suppliers with no formal security governance | Supplier register, risk assessments per supplier, contractual security clauses, review schedule |
| 8.24 | Use of cryptography | Likely gaps in telehealth data-in-transit and data-at-rest encryption evidence | Cryptography policy, TLS configs, Azure disk/storage encryption proof, key management procedure |
| 5.24–5.28 | Incident management | ITIL incident process exists but may not meet ISO evidence bar | Incident classification including security events, escalation to MSSP, root-cause analysis, breach notification procedure (also HIPAA) |
| 5.34 | Privacy / PII | Healthcare = PHI everywhere | PII inventory, DPIAs or equivalent, mapping to HIPAA Privacy & Security Rule — auditors will probe this |

**HIPAA Crossover (do alongside, not separately)**

| HIPAA requirement | ISO 27001 mapping | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Security risk analysis (§164.308(a)(1)) | Clause 6.1.2 + Annex A 5.9, 8.8 | Single risk assessment satisfying both |
| BAA with MSSP and SaaS vendors | Annex A 5.19–5.22 | Confirm BAAs in place, attach to supplier register |
| Access controls / unique user IDs | Annex A 5.15, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5 | Evidence from Azure AD / Entra ID, EHR access logs |
| Audit logs / monitoring | Annex A 8.15, 8.16 | MSSP SOC log retention, review cadence |
| Breach notification (60-day rule) | Annex A 5.24–5.28 | Documented procedure, test it |

---

### 🟡 MEDIUM PRIORITY — Build out in parallel

| Ref | Control area | Gap | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.3 | Awareness & training | Likely ad-hoc | Annual security awareness programme with completion records, role-based training for IT staff and clinicians |
| 5.30 | ICT readiness for business continuity | Probably no tested DR plan for Azure/EHR outage | BCP/DR plan, RPO/RTO definitions, test results (tabletop at minimum) |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | CMDB incomplete, likely no hardening baselines | Azure/server baseline configs (CIS benchmarks), documented standard builds |
| 8.32 | Change management | ITIL change process exists — formalise and evidence | Change policy referencing security impact assessment, CAB/approval records, link to CMDB |
| 8.1 | User endpoint devices | BYOD policy exists but enforcement unclear | MDM/MAM evidence (Intune), conditional access policies, BYOD enrolment records |
| 5.15, 8.2, 8.5 | Access control / privileged access | Likely exists but may lack periodic reviews | Access control policy, quarterly access reviews, PAM tooling or procedure for admin accounts |
| 8.13 | Backup | Probably in place, may lack testing evidence | Backup policy with RPO, automated backup configs, restore test logs (quarterly) |

---

### 🟢 LOW PRIORITY — Polish before Stage 2

| Ref | Control area | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 5.23 | Information security for cloud services | Document shared-responsibility model for Azure + each SaaS app |
| 5.4 | Management responsibilities | Formal role descriptions for ISMS roles (information security manager, risk owner, asset owners) |
| 5.35 | Independent review of information security | Plan for surveillance-year activity; not needed before initial cert |
| 8.25–8.28 | Secure development | Relevant only if you build telehealth software in-house; if SaaS, document vendor SDLC assurance |
| 7.1–7.14 | Physical controls | Clinic physical access, server room, visitor logs — usually straightforward |

---

## 2. Highest-Priority Gaps → IT Manager Deliverables

| Gap | What the IT manager must deliver | Cadence / deadline |
|---|---|---|
| **CMDB / asset register** | Complete inventory of all hardware, cloud subscriptions, SaaS apps, data stores, with assigned owners | Complete within 4–6 weeks, then continuous updates via change process |
| **Risk register** | Facilitate risk workshops with clinical and IT stakeholders, populate register, propose treatment options, present to management for acceptance | Initial pass in 6–8 weeks; review quarterly |
| **Vulnerability management programme** | Select scanner (e.g., Defender for Cloud, Qualys), define scan schedule (monthly minimum + post-change), set remediation SLAs (Critical ≤ 48 h, High ≤ 7 d, Medium ≤ 30 d), track closure | Monthly reporting to management review |
| **Supplier security governance** | Build supplier register, verify BAAs, collect SOC 2 / ISO 27001 certs from MSSP and EHR vendor, schedule annual reviews | Register in 4 weeks; reviews annually |
| **Incident response procedure** | Revise ITIL incident process to include security classification, MSSP escalation matrix, evidence preservation steps, HIPAA breach notification timeline | Document in 4 weeks; tabletop test quarterly |
| **Policy suite** | Draft or upgrade: ISMS policy, access control, cryptography, data classification, VM, backup, supplier security, BCP/DR, BYOD (expand existing) | 6–8 weeks for drafts; approval by management |
| **Evidence of change management** | Ensure every RFC includes a security impact field; archive CAB minutes and approval artefacts | Ongoing — start immediately |
| **Internal audit** | Plan and schedule (or outsource) internal audit of ISMS; track NCRs to closure | At least one full cycle before Stage 2 |
| **Management review** | Prepare agenda and inputs pack (risk status, audit results, incident trends, MSSP reports), schedule with leadership | Quarterly recommended, minimum annual |

---

## 3. MSSP / SOC Onboarding Checklist for ISO Evidence

Give this to your MSSP relationship manager and bake it into the contract or service schedule.

**Contractual and governance**

- [ ] BAA executed (HIPAA requirement)
- [ ] Security roles and responsibilities documented in service agreement
- [ ] MSSP's own ISO 27001 or SOC 2 Type II report obtained and reviewed annually
- [ ] Escalation matrix with named contacts, severity definitions aligned to your incident classification
- [ ] Right-to-audit clause or equivalent assurance commitment

**Detection and monitoring evidence**

- [ ] Monthly SOC summary report covering: alerts triaged, incidents escalated, false-positive rate, mean-time-to-detect, mean-time-to-respond
- [ ] Log sources confirmed: Azure activity logs, Entra ID sign-ins, EHR audit logs, endpoint EDR, firewall/NSG, VPN
- [ ] Minimum log retention period agreed and documented (≥ 12 months recommended, check HIPAA 6-year retention for audit logs)
- [ ] Evidence of 24/7 coverage (shift rosters or SLA commitment)

**Incident handling**

- [ ] MSSP follows your incident response procedure, not just their own
- [ ] Security incidents reported to you within agreed SLA (e.g., P1 ≤ 15 min notification)
- [ ] Root-cause analysis delivered for all P1/P2 incidents
- [ ] MSSP preserves forensic evidence and chain-of-custody documentation
- [ ] MSSP supports your HIPAA breach determination process (provides data needed for breach risk assessment)

**Vulnerability and threat intelligence**

- [ ] MSSP provides or feeds threat intel relevant to healthcare sector
- [ ] If MSSP runs scans on your behalf: scan reports delivered per your VM policy cadence, findings in a format you can import into your risk register

**Audit and compliance**

- [ ] MSSP provides evidence packs on request for ISO internal/external audits (e.g., alert handling records, change logs on SIEM rules)
- [ ] Annual service review meeting documented with minutes (feeds into your management review)
- [ ] MSSP notifies you of any security incidents within their own environment that could affect your data

---

**Suggested next steps from here:**

1. **Assign an ISMS lead** (can be you or a consultant) and get management sign-off on the project.
2. **Tackle the CMDB and risk assessment simultaneously** — they feed each other.
3. **Send the MSSP checklist this week** — long lead items like contract amendments and evidence format changes take time.

Want me to drill into any of these — for example, a risk assessment template, a policy outline, or a detailed HIPAA-to-ISO control map?

# 1. Risk Assessment Workshop Template

## Instructions for the workshop facilitator

- **Pre-work**: circulate the asset register (even incomplete) and ask attendees to bring their top-5 "what keeps you up at night" scenarios.
- **Attendees**: IT manager, clinical lead, privacy officer, MSSP contact (optional), one member of senior leadership (risk owner authority).
- **Duration**: 2–3 hours for initial pass; aim for 15–25 risks in the first session.
- **Tool**: spreadsheet is fine — no need for GRC software yet.

## Template columns

Copy this header row into your spreadsheet:

```
Risk ID | Asset / Process | Threat | Vulnerability | Consequence | Likelihood (1–5) | Impact (1–5) | Risk Score (L×I) | Risk Level | Treatment Option | Planned Controls | Owner | Target Date | Residual Risk (L×I) | Status
```

### Scoring definitions

**Likelihood**

| Score | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | < once per 5 years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Once per 2–5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Once per 1–2 years |
| 4 | Likely | Several times per year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Monthly or more |

**Impact** (tailor the descriptors to healthcare)

| Score | Label | Patient safety | Data breach scope | Financial | Regulatory |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | None | < 10 records | < $10 K | Informal query |
| 2 | Minor | Discomfort, no harm | 10–100 records | $10–50 K | Letter of concern |
| 3 | Moderate | Temporary harm | 100–1 000 records | $50–250 K | Formal investigation |
| 4 | Major | Serious harm | 1 000–5 000 records | $250 K–1 M | Enforcement action / fine |
| 5 | Catastrophic | Death / permanent harm | > 5 000 records or public leak of PHI | > $1 M | OCR resolution agreement / loss of licence |

**Risk level matrix**

| | Impact 1 | Impact 2 | Impact 3 | Impact 4 | Impact 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Likelihood 5** | 5 M | 10 H | 15 H | 20 C | 25 C |
| **Likelihood 4** | 4 M | 8 M | 12 H | 16 H | 20 C |
| **Likelihood 3** | 3 L | 6 M | 9 M | 12 H | 15 H |
| **Likelihood 2** | 2 L | 4 M | 6 M | 8 M | 10 H |
| **Likelihood 1** | 1 L | 2 L | 3 L | 4 M | 5 M |

> **L** = Low (accept/monitor) · **M** = Medium (treat within 90 days) · **H** = High (treat within 30 days) · **C** = Critical (immediate action)

**Treatment options** (use these exact labels for consistency)

| Code | Option | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Mitigate** | Apply or improve controls | Default for most risks |
| **Transfer** | Insure or contractually shift | Cyber insurance, MSSP SLA |
| **Avoid** | Stop the activity | Activity not essential |
| **Accept** | Formally accept with management sign-off | Residual risk within appetite |

### Worked example row

```
R-007 | Telehealth platform | Interception of video consult | No end-to-end encryption verified | PHI disclosure, HIPAA breach | 3 | 4 | 12 | HIGH | Mitigate | Verify TLS 1.2+, enable E2EE, document in cryptography policy | IT Manager | 2026-06-30 | 2×4 = 8 M | In progress
```

### After the workshop

1. Sort by risk score descending.
2. Get the designated risk owner (must have authority) to sign off on each treatment decision.
3. Present the top-10 risks and treatment plan to leadership as your first management review input.
4. Store the register as a controlled document — version it.

---

# 2. Statement of Applicability (SoA) Skeleton

## SoA metadata header

```
Organisation : [Clinic name]
ISMS Scope : [Copy from scope statement]
ISO 27001:2022 Annex A version: 2022 (93 controls)
SoA Version : 1.0
Prepared by : [Name / role]
Approved by : [Top management name]
Date : [Date]
Risk treatment plan ref : [Document ID]
```

## Column structure

```
Annex A Ref | Control Title | Applicable? (Y/N) | Justification for Inclusion or Exclusion | Implementation Status | Implementation Evidence / Notes | Linked Risk IDs
```

### How to handle exclusions (auditors look at this closely)

Rules:

- You may **only exclude controls** that do not relate to risks identified in your risk assessment and do not affect your ability to meet ISMS requirements.
- You **cannot exclude mandatory clauses** (4–10) — only Annex A controls.
- Every exclusion needs a **documented justification**, not just "N/A."

**Good exclusion example:**

```
8.28 | Secure coding | N | Organisation does not develop software. EHR and telehealth are SaaS; vendor SDLC assurance obtained under supplier management (5.19–5.22). | — | Vendor SOC 2 report on file. | —
```

**Bad exclusion (will trigger auditor finding):**

```
8.28 | Secure coding | N | Not applicable. | — | — | —
```

## Starter rows (pre-populated for your context)

Below are examples across all four Annex A themes. Populate the remaining controls the same way.

### Theme 5 — Organisational controls (37 controls)

```
5.1  | Policies for information security        | Y | Required ISMS foundation                                      | Partial | AUP and BYOD exist; overarching ISMS policy in draft            | R-001
5.9  | Inventory of information and other assets | Y | Foundation for risk assessment; HIPAA asset requirement         | Partial | CMDB project in progress (target 2026-07-15)                    | R-003, R-012
5.10 | Acceptable use of information             | Y | PHI handling, endpoint use                                     | Implemented | AUP v2.1 signed by all staff                                | R-005
5.19 | Information security in supplier relations | Y | MSSP and EHR vendor are critical suppliers                     | Partial | BAAs in place; supplier register being built                    | R-007
5.24 | Incident management planning              | Y | HIPAA breach notification obligation                           | Partial | ITIL incident process exists; security classification in draft  | R-010
```

### Theme 6 — People controls (8 controls)

```
6.1  | Screening                                 | Y | Healthcare staff handle PHI                                    | Implemented | Background checks via HR                                    | R-014
6.3  | Awareness, education and training         | Y | Regulatory and risk requirement                                | Gap       | No formal programme; planned Q3 2026                            | R-015
```

### Theme 7 — Physical controls (14 controls)

```
7.1  | Physical security perimeters              | Y | Clinic premises, server room                                   | Implemented | Access-controlled entry, alarm system                       | R-018
7.4  | Physical security monitoring              | Y | Clinic and server room                                         | Implemented | CCTV, 30-day retention                                      | R-018
```

### Theme 8 — Technological controls (34 controls)

```
8.2  | Privileged access rights                  | Y | Azure admin, EHR admin accounts                               | Partial | Entra ID PIM configured; quarterly reviews not yet scheduled    | R-006
8.8  | Management of technical vulnerabilities   | Y | Critical gap identified in risk assessment                     | Gap       | VM programme design in progress                                 | R-004
8.13 | Information backup                        | Y | RPO/RTO needed for EHR and telehealth                          | Partial | Azure backup configured; restore tests not documented           | R-020
8.15 | Logging                                   | Y | Audit trail for PHI access                                     | Implemented | MSSP ingests logs; retention 12 months                      | R-010
8.24 | Use of cryptography                       | Y | PHI at rest and in transit                                     | Partial | TLS enforced; disk encryption on; key management undocumented   | R-007
8.28 | Secure coding                             | N | No in-house development; EHR and telehealth are SaaS. Vendor SDLC assurance reviewed under 5.19–5.22. | — | Vendor SOC 2 on file | —
```

> Populate all 93 rows using this pattern. The auditor will read every row.

---

# 3. CMDB Completion Checklist — 4 to 6 Weeks

## Week 1 — Discover and scope

- [ ] Define what "asset" means for your ISMS (hardware, software, cloud services, data stores, network, people roles, facilities)
- [ ] Choose your CMDB tool — existing ITSM tool (ServiceNow, Freshservice, etc.) or even a controlled spreadsheet for now
- [ ] Define the minimum attribute set per asset type:

```
  Asset ID | Name | Type | Owner | Location (physical / cloud region) |
  Criticality (High / Med / Low) | Data classification it handles |
  Support contract / vendor | IP / URL | Relationships / dependencies
```

- [ ] Run automated discovery against Azure (Resource Graph / Defender for Cloud inventory export) and on-prem (network scan, AD computer objects)
- [ ] Export EHR vendor's asset list from your SaaS admin console
- [ ] Pull a list of all SaaS subscriptions (check SSO portal, Entra ID enterprise apps, expense reports for shadow IT)

## Week 2 — Assign owners and classify

- [ ] Assign an **owner** to every discovered asset (a person, not a team)
- [ ] Walk asset list with department heads — 30-min meetings per department: clinical, admin, finance, IT
- [ ] Flag any asset that stores, processes, or transmits PHI → auto-classify as **Confidential** minimum
- [ ] Identify orphan assets (no owner, unknown purpose) → investigate or decommission
- [ ] Mark asset criticality based on impact if unavailable for > 4 hours

## Week 3 — Map relationships and dependencies

- [ ] Document dependencies: which apps depend on which infrastructure (e.g., EHR → internet link + Azure AD + endpoint devices)
- [ ] Map data flows for PHI: where does PHI enter, get stored, get transmitted, leave the org
- [ ] Link MSSP-managed assets (SIEM, EDR console) into the register with MSSP as operator, you as owner
- [ ] Record network segments / VLANs and what sits on each

## Week 4 — Validate and plug gaps

- [ ] Reconcile discovery scan results against manual register — find deltas
- [ ] Confirm on-prem server list against hypervisor inventory and rack audit
- [ ] Verify Azure resource groups against register (look for rogue subscriptions)
- [ ] Walk the clinic physically — check for unregistered switches, access points, printers, medical IoT devices
- [ ] Add mobile / BYOD device count from Intune / MDM

## Week 5 — Formalise and connect to ISMS

- [ ] Link each asset to relevant risks in the risk register (column: Linked Risk IDs)
- [ ] Confirm every Annex A 5.9 attribute is populated — auditor will sample check
- [ ] Define the update process: CMDB updated as part of change management (every RFC must reference affected CIs)
- [ ] Document the CMDB policy or procedure (can be a section in your asset management policy)
- [ ] Get IT manager sign-off on completeness; present summary to management review

## Week 6 — Buffer and ongoing hygiene

- [ ] Catch-up week for stragglers
- [ ] Schedule recurring tasks:
  - Monthly: automated re-scan vs CMDB reconciliation
  - Quarterly: owner review (are owners still correct?)
  - Annually: full CMDB audit as internal audit input
- [ ] Feed final asset register into the SoA and risk assessment — close the loop

### Quick win metrics to report upward

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| % of assets with assigned owner | 100 % |
| % of PHI-touching assets identified | 100 % |
| Orphan assets resolved | 0 remaining |
| Mean time to update CMDB after change | ≤ 2 business days |

---

**Where to go next — pick any:**

- Policy template pack (ISMS policy, access control, cryptography, etc.)
- HIPAA-to-ISO 27001 detailed control crosswalk
- Internal audit plan and checklist for first cycle
- Board / leadership slide deck to get ISMS project formally approved

# ISO 27001 Policy Template Pack

> **Usage notes**
> - Replace all `[bracketed]` placeholders before publishing.
> - Each policy must be version-controlled, approved by management, and communicated to relevant staff.
> - Store in a central, access-controlled document repository (SharePoint, Confluence, etc.).
> - Review cycle: at least annual or after significant change.

---

## Policy 0 — Document Control Header (use on every policy)

```
Document ID    : [POL-ISMS-001]
Title          : [Policy title]
Version        : [1.0]
Classification : Internal
Owner          : [Role, e.g., IT Manager / CISO]
Approved by    : [Senior management name and title]
Approval date  : [Date]
Next review    : [Date — max 12 months]
Distribution   : [All staff / IT department / named roles]
Change history :
  Version | Date | Author | Changes
  1.0     |      |        | Initial release
```

---

## Policy 1 — Information Security Management System (ISMS) Policy

**ISO references**: Clauses 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 · Annex A 5.1

### 1 Purpose

This policy establishes [Organisation name]'s commitment to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information — including protected health information (PHI) — through a formal ISMS conforming to ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

### 2 Scope

The ISMS applies to:

- All information assets within the defined scope: [clinic operations, telehealth service, Azure cloud environment, on-premises infrastructure, SaaS applications including EHR, outsourced SOC].
- All employees, contractors, and third parties who access organisational information.

### 3 Objectives

- Protect patient and corporate data against unauthorised access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction.
- Comply with applicable legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations including HIPAA.
- Manage information security risks to an acceptable level defined by management.
- Continually improve the ISMS through measurement and review.

### 4 Leadership commitment

Senior management commits to:

- Providing resources for ISMS implementation and operation.
- Setting and reviewing information security objectives annually.
- Conducting management reviews at least [quarterly / annually].
- Promoting continual improvement.

### 5 Roles and responsibilities

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| [CEO / Clinic Director] | Accountable for ISMS; approves risk appetite and policies |
| [IT Manager / CISO] | Operates the ISMS; manages risk register, SoA, internal audits |
| [Privacy Officer] | HIPAA compliance, breach determination |
| Asset owners | Manage risks to their assets; approve access |
| All staff | Comply with policies; report incidents |

### 6 Risk management

Information security risks shall be identified, assessed, treated, and monitored per the Risk Assessment Procedure [ref]. Risk acceptance requires documented approval from management.

### 7 Policy framework

This overarching policy is supported by topic-specific policies: access control, data classification, incident response, supplier security, vulnerability management, backup and DR, and BYOD/MDM.

### 8 Compliance and enforcement

Violations may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination and legal proceedings.

### 9 Review

This policy is reviewed at least annually or following significant changes to the organisation, technology, or threat landscape.

**Audit evidence examples**: signed policy, management review minutes, risk appetite statement, ISMS scope document.

**HIPAA alignment**: satisfies the administrative safeguard requirement for a security management process (§164.308(a)(1)) and assigned security responsibility (§164.308(a)(2)).

---

## Policy 2 — Access Control

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.15, 5.16, 5.17, 5.18, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

### 1 Purpose

Ensure that access to information and systems is authorised, appropriate, and reviewable.

### 2 Principles

- **Least privilege**: users receive the minimum access required for their role.
- **Need-to-know**: access to PHI only when required for job function.
- **Segregation of duties**: no single person controls all stages of a critical process.

### 3 User access lifecycle

| Stage | Requirement | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Request** | Formal access request approved by asset owner | Ticket / form in ITSM |
| **Provisioning** | Based on role-based access profiles in Entra ID / EHR | Entra ID group membership logs |
| **Review** | Quarterly review of all access rights by asset owners | Signed review spreadsheet or tool export |
| **Revocation** | Same-day disable on termination; next business day on role change | HR notification → IT ticket → Entra ID audit log |

### 4 Privileged access

- Privileged accounts managed via Entra ID PIM (just-in-time activation, approval required, time-limited).
- Separate admin accounts — no daily work on privileged credentials.
- All privileged sessions logged and reviewed monthly.

### 5 Authentication

- MFA enforced for all users on all cloud services and VPN.
- Password policy: minimum 14 characters, complexity, 90-day rotation or passwordless alternative.
- Service accounts: managed identities or vaulted secrets; no shared passwords.

### 6 Remote and telehealth access

- VPN or Azure conditional access policy required.
- Device compliance check (managed device, patched, encrypted) before access granted.

### 7 Review and audit

Access reviews conducted quarterly. Results documented and exceptions remediated within 14 days.

**Audit evidence examples**: Entra ID conditional access policy exports, PIM activation logs, quarterly access review records, joiner/mover/leaver tickets.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.312(a)(1) access control, §164.312(d) authentication, §164.312(a)(2)(i) unique user ID, §164.312(a)(2)(iii) automatic logoff.

---

## Policy 3 — Data Classification and Handling

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, 5.33, 5.34, 8.10, 8.11, 8.12

### 1 Classification levels

| Level | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Restricted** | Severe harm if disclosed; legal/regulatory obligation | PHI, ePHI, psychotherapy notes, financial account data |
| **Confidential** | Business harm if disclosed | Employee HR records, contracts, internal audit reports |
| **Internal** | Not sensitive but not for public release | Staff newsletters, internal procedures, meeting notes |
| **Public** | Approved for unrestricted distribution | Marketing materials, published policies |

### 2 Labelling

- Documents: classification label in header/footer.
- Emails containing Restricted data: sensitivity label applied via Microsoft Purview / equivalent.
- Cloud storage: Azure Information Protection labels or container-level tagging.

### 3 Handling rules

| Activity | Restricted (PHI) | Confidential | Internal | Public |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Storage | Encrypted at rest (AES-256); access-controlled | Encrypted or access-controlled | Access-controlled | No restriction |
| Transmission | TLS 1.2+ or VPN; encrypted email | TLS 1.2+ | Standard email OK | No restriction |
| Printing | Collect immediately; secure shred when done | Secure shred | Recycle bin OK | No restriction |
| Sharing external | Only via approved, encrypted channel; BAA required | NDA required | Management approval | Freely |
| Disposal | Crypto-erase / NIST 800-88 media sanitisation | Secure delete | Standard delete | Standard delete |
| Retention | Per HIPAA (6 years for policies; state law for medical records) | Per retention schedule | Per retention schedule | No minimum |

### 4 PHI-specific requirements

- PHI inventory maintained and linked to asset register.
- Minimum necessary standard applied to every access and disclosure.
- De-identification follows HIPAA Safe Harbor or Expert Determination method when sharing for secondary purposes.

### 5 Responsibilities

Data owners classify their data at creation. All staff handle data according to its classification. IT manager enforces technical controls.

**Audit evidence examples**: classification policy, labelling screenshots, Purview/AIP config exports, sample classified documents, PHI inventory, media destruction certificates.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption and decryption, §164.530(j) retention, §164.514 de-identification, §164.502(b) minimum necessary.

## Policy 4 — Incident Response and Breach Notification

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.24, 5.25, 5.26, 5.27, 5.28, 6.8

### 1 Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Security event** | Observable occurrence that may affect information security |
| **Security incident** | Event that has actually compromised CIA of information |
| **Breach (HIPAA)** | Unauthorised acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of unsecured PHI |

### 2 Severity classification

| Severity | Criteria | Response SLA | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P1 — Critical** | Active data exfil, ransomware, PHI breach confirmed | Immediate; all-hands | Ransomware on EHR server, mass PHI leak |
| **P2 — High** | Likely compromise, service outage affecting patient care | ≤ 1 hour | Compromised admin account, EHR down |
| **P3 — Medium** | Contained incident, no PHI exposure confirmed | ≤ 4 hours | Phishing with credential entry, malware on single endpoint |
| **P4 — Low** | Near-miss, policy violation | ≤ 24 hours | Misdirected internal email, failed brute-force |

### 3 Response process

```
Detect → Triage → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Lessons learned
```

| Phase | Actions | Responsible |
|---|---|---|
| **Detect** | MSSP SOC alert, staff report, automated tool alert | MSSP / All staff |
| **Triage** | Classify severity, assign incident lead, open ITSM ticket | IT Manager |
| **Contain** | Isolate affected systems, disable compromised accounts, preserve evidence | IT Manager + MSSP |
| **Eradicate** | Remove threat actor/malware, patch vulnerability, reset credentials | IT team + MSSP |
| **Recover** | Restore from backup, confirm integrity, monitor closely | IT team |
| **Lessons learned** | Post-incident review within 5 business days, update risk register and controls | IT Manager |

### 4 HIPAA breach notification procedure

```
Step 1 → Determine if unsecured PHI was involved
Step 2 → Conduct 4-factor breach risk assessment:
           (a) Nature and extent of PHI involved
           (b) Unauthorised person who accessed or received PHI
           (c) Whether PHI was actually acquired or viewed
           (d) Extent of risk mitigation
Step 3 → If breach is not excluded by risk assessment:
           • Individual notice: ≤ 60 calendar days from discovery
           • HHS/OCR notice: ≤ 60 days (if ≥ 500 individuals: also notify media)
           • If < 500 individuals: log and report annually to HHS
Step 4 → Document determination and rationale regardless of outcome
Step 5 → Notify [Privacy Officer] immediately upon suspicion of PHI involvement
```

### 5 Evidence preservation

- Do not reboot or reimage affected systems until forensic image taken or MSSP confirms evidence captured.
- Screenshot alerts, timestamps, affected accounts.
- Maintain chain-of-custody log for any physical media.

### 6 Communication

| Audience | Channel | Authorised by |
|---|---|---|
| Internal staff | Email / meeting | IT Manager |
| Patients / individuals | Written notice per HIPAA | Privacy Officer + Legal |
| HHS/OCR | HHS breach portal | Privacy Officer |
| Media (if ≥ 500) | Press statement | [CEO / Legal] |
| Cyber insurer | Per policy terms | [CFO / IT Manager] |

### 7 Testing

Tabletop exercise at least twice per year; one scenario must involve PHI breach. Document results and corrective actions.

**Audit evidence examples**: incident log / ITSM tickets, MSSP alert reports, post-incident reviews, breach risk assessment forms, breach notification letters (redacted), tabletop exercise records.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(6) security incident procedures, §164.404–408 breach notification rule.

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.19, 5.20, 5.21, 5.22, 5.23

### 1 Supplier classification

| Tier | Criteria | Examples | Review cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | Processes or stores PHI; outage directly impacts patient care | EHR vendor, MSSP, Azure (Microsoft) | Every 6 months |
| **Important** | Access to internal data or systems; moderate impact | Payroll SaaS, email filtering, ISP | Annually |

### 2 Supplier register

Maintain a register with: supplier name, service, tier, data accessed, contract expiry, BAA status, last review date, security certification held.

### 3 Security requirements in contracts

- [ ] Confidentiality / NDA clause
- [ ] Right-to-audit or evidence of independent audit (SOC 2 / ISO 27001)

- [ ] Data return / destruction on termination

- Collect and review SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate annually for Critical and Important suppliers.
- Review MSSP monthly reports against contractual SLAs.
- Track supplier-related incidents in the incident register.
- Include supplier risk in the organisational risk register.

For Azure and SaaS services:

- Document shared-responsibility model per service (IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS).

# Policy 6 (continued) — Vulnerability Management

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.8, 8.7, 8.32

### 1 Scope

All assets in the ISMS scope: Azure resources, on-prem servers, endpoints, network devices, SaaS configurations.

### 2 Vulnerability identification

| Source | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Automated infrastructure scanning (Defender for Cloud / Qualys) | Weekly minimum; daily for internet-facing assets |
| Application scanning (DAST / SaaS config review) | Monthly |
| Annual penetration test (third-party) | Annually + after major architecture change |
| Vendor advisories and CVE feeds | Continuous (automated alerting) |
| MSSP threat intelligence | Continuous |

### 3 Severity rating and remediation SLAs

Use CVSS v3+ base score, then adjust for environmental context (PHI exposure, internet-facing, exploitability).

| Rating | CVSS range | Remediation SLA | Approval to defer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | 9.0–10.0 | ≤ 48 hours | [CISO / IT Manager] only, documented risk acceptance |
| **High** | 7.0–8.9 | ≤ 7 calendar days | IT Manager approval |
| **Medium** | 4.0–6.9 | ≤ 30 calendar days | Standard change process |
| **Low** | 0.1–3.9 | ≤ 90 calendar days or next patch cycle | Batch with scheduled maintenance |

### 4 Remediation process

```
Scan → Triage → Prioritise → Remediate/Mitigate → Verify → Close
```

- All remediation tracked as ITSM tickets linked to the vulnerability scan finding.
- Patches follow the change management process (RFC with security impact field).
- Where patching is not possible, document compensating control and risk acceptance in the risk register.
- Re-scan to verify remediation within 5 business days of fix.

### 5 Emergency patching

For actively exploited zero-days affecting PHI systems, the IT Manager may authorise emergency change outside normal CAB, with retrospective documentation within 24 hours.

### 6 Reporting

| Report | Audience | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| Scan results and open findings | IT team | Weekly |
| KPI dashboard (mean-time-to-remediate, overdue count, trend) | Management review | Monthly |
| Pen test report and remediation tracker | Senior management | Annually |

### 7 Exceptions

Any vulnerability exceeding its SLA must have a documented exception with: justification, compensating controls, risk owner approval, and expiry date (maximum 90 days, then re-evaluate).

**Audit evidence examples**: scan reports, remediation tickets with timestamps, pen test report and remediation tracker, exception approvals, KPI dashboard, emergency change records.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) risk management implementation, §164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B) protection from malicious software.

> **Quick evidence checklist for auditors (hand this over):**
> 1. Last three monthly scan reports with finding counts and closure rates
> 2. Sample of five remediation tickets showing scan-to-close lifecycle
> 3. Most recent pen test report plus remediation status tracker
> 4. Any active exception forms with risk owner sign-off
> 5. KPI trend chart (mean-time-to-remediate by severity, last 6 months)

# Policy 7 — Backup and Disaster Recovery

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30

### 1 Purpose

Ensure information and systems can be restored within defined timeframes to maintain patient care continuity and protect PHI integrity.

### 2 Scope

All systems within the ISMS scope: Azure-hosted services, on-prem servers, EHR (SaaS — vendor-managed backup confirmed separately), endpoint configurations, identity directory (Entra ID).

### 3 Backup requirements by asset criticality

| Asset class | RPO | RTO | Backup method | Retention |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EHR database** (SaaS) | Per vendor SLA (verify ≤ 1 hr) | Per vendor SLA (verify ≤ 4 hrs) | Vendor-managed; confirm in BAA and supplier review | Per vendor + local export monthly |
| **Azure workloads** (VMs, PaaS databases) | ≤ 4 hours | ≤ 8 hours | Azure Backup vault, geo-redundant (GRS) | 30 daily, 12 monthly, 7 yearly |
| **On-prem servers** | ≤ 24 hours | ≤ 24 hours | Azure Backup agent or equivalent to offsite vault | 30 daily, 12 monthly |
| **Entra ID / M365 config** | ≤ 24 hours | ≤ 8 hours | Third-party SaaS backup tool (e.g., Veeam for M365) | 12 months |
| **Network device configs** | At every change | ≤ 4 hours | Automated config backup to secured repo | Last 10 versions |
| **Endpoint (SOE image)** | N/A — rebuild | ≤ 4 hours | Standard image + Intune policy re-push | Current image always available |

### 4 Backup security

- All backup data encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+).
- Backup storage access restricted to named backup administrators only.
- Backup credentials stored in a secrets vault, rotated every 90 days.
- At least one backup copy stored in a separate Azure region or offsite location (3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite).
- Immutable / WORM backup enabled for ransomware resilience where supported.

### 5 Restore testing

| Test type | Scope | Cadence | Documented output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Individual file restore** | Random sample from each asset class | Monthly | Restore log with timestamp, integrity hash comparison |
| **Full system restore** | One critical system (rotate quarterly) | Quarterly | Restore report: time taken vs RTO, data integrity verified |
| **Tabletop DR exercise** | End-to-end scenario (e.g., ransomware, Azure region outage) | Twice per year | Exercise report, action items, lessons learned |
| **Full DR failover** (if DR environment exists) | All critical systems | Annually | Failover and failback report |

### 6 Disaster recovery plan summary

| Phase | Actions | Responsible |
|---|---|---|
| **Activation** | Incident declared P1; DR lead notified; communication tree activated | IT Manager / CISO |
| **Assessment** | Determine scope of outage, estimate recovery time, notify leadership | IT Manager |
| **Recovery** | Execute restore / failover per runbooks; prioritise by RTO | IT team |
| **Validation** | Confirm data integrity, application functionality, PHI availability | IT team + clinical lead |
| **Return to normal** | Failback to primary, full backup, post-incident review | IT team |
| **Lessons learned** | Document within 5 business days; update risk register and runbooks | IT Manager |

### 7 Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| IT Manager | DR plan owner, authorises activation, reports to leadership |
| Backup administrator | Configures and monitors backups, executes restores |
| MSSP | Monitors backup job alerts (if in scope), supports forensic recovery |
| Clinical lead | Validates clinical system functionality post-restore |
| EHR vendor | Executes SaaS-side restores per BAA obligations |

### 8 Review

DR plan and runbooks reviewed annually and after every DR activation or significant infrastructure change. Restore test results feed into management review.

**Audit evidence examples**: backup configuration screenshots, backup job success/failure logs, restore test reports with integrity verification, DR tabletop exercise report, DR plan document with version history, vendor SLA confirmation for EHR backups.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(7) contingency plan (data backup plan, disaster recovery plan, emergency mode operation plan, testing and revision procedures).

> **Quick evidence checklist for auditors (hand this over):**
> 1. Last three months of backup job success/failure reports (all asset classes)
> 2. Most recent quarterly full-system restore test report with RTO comparison
> 3. Latest tabletop DR exercise report and action tracker
> 4. EHR vendor SLA / BAA section confirming vendor backup and RPO/RTO
> 5. Backup encryption and access control configuration evidence

# Policy 8 — BYOD and Mobile Device Management

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.1, 6.7, 8.10, 8.11, 8.12

### 1 Purpose

Enable staff to use personal and mobile devices for work while protecting organisational information and PHI from loss, theft, or unauthorised access.

### 2 Scope

All personally owned devices (smartphones, tablets, laptops) and organisation-issued mobile devices used to access organisational email, applications, or data, including telehealth platforms.

### 3 Enrolment requirements

Before accessing any organisational resource, every device must:

- [ ] Be registered in the MDM/MAM platform (Microsoft Intune or equivalent)
- [ ] Meet minimum OS version: iOS [17+], Android [14+], Windows [11 23H2+]
- [ ] Have device encryption enabled (FileVault, BitLocker, or native Android/iOS encryption)
- [ ] Have screen lock configured (biometric or PIN ≥ 6 digits, auto-lock ≤ 2 minutes)
- [ ] Pass a compliance check before conditional access grants a token

### 4 Conditional access policy (enforced via Entra ID)

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Device compliance | Must pass Intune compliance policy (encrypted, patched, not jailbroken) |
| MFA | Required on every authentication from personal device |
| Location | Access from approved countries only; block high-risk locations |
| App protection | MAM policy wraps corporate apps: cut/copy/paste restricted to managed apps, save-to-personal-storage blocked |
| Session | Re-authentication every [12 hours]; revoke on compliance failure |

### 5 Permitted and prohibited activities

| Permitted | Prohibited |
|---|---|
| Email and calendar via Outlook (managed) | Storing PHI in personal apps, personal cloud storage, or local unmanaged folders |
| EHR access via approved app / browser with MAM policy | Screenshots of PHI (enforced via app protection policy where possible) |
| Telehealth consultations via approved platform | Use of jailbroken / rooted devices |
| Teams messaging and calls | Sharing device credentials with family members or third parties |
| VPN access from compliant device | Connecting to organisational resources from public Wi-Fi without VPN |

### 6 Data segregation

- Corporate data containerised within managed apps (Intune App Protection).
- Organisation cannot view personal photos, messages, or apps.
- On unenrolment or wipe, only the corporate container is removed; personal data untouched (selective wipe).

### 7 Lost, stolen, or compromised device

| Step | Action | SLA |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | User reports loss/theft to IT service desk immediately | ≤ 1 hour from discovery |
| 2 | IT initiates remote selective wipe of corporate container | ≤ 2 hours from report |
| 3 | Entra ID sign-in sessions revoked, device marked non-compliant | Immediate |
| 4 | If PHI exposure suspected, escalate to incident response procedure (Policy 4) | Per incident severity SLA |
| 5 | Log event in ITSM and incident register | Same day |

### 8 Staff responsibilities

- Keep device OS and apps updated within [14 days] of patch release.
- Do not disable MDM/MAM profiles.
- Report loss, theft, or suspected compromise immediately.
- Consent to corporate container management as a condition of BYOD access (documented at enrolment).

### 9 Monitoring and compliance

- Intune compliance dashboard reviewed weekly by IT.
- Non-compliant devices automatically blocked from corporate resources via conditional access.
- Quarterly report on BYOD fleet: enrolment count, compliance rate, wipe events, OS version distribution.

### 10 Exit process

On employment termination:

- Selective wipe triggered on termination day (linked to HR leaver process and access revocation in Policy 2).
- Device unenrolled from Intune.
- User confirms removal of any residual corporate data.

**Audit evidence examples**: Intune compliance policy configuration export, conditional access policy screenshots, MAM/app protection policy settings, device compliance dashboard, selective wipe logs, signed BYOD user consent forms, quarterly fleet compliance report.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.310(d)(1) device and media controls, §164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption, §164.312(d) person or entity authentication, §164.310(d)(2)(iii) accountability for device tracking.

> **Quick evidence checklist for auditors (hand this over):**
> 1. Intune compliance and conditional access policy exports (screenshots or JSON)
> 2. Sample of signed BYOD enrolment / consent forms
> 3. Last quarter's device compliance dashboard (compliance rate, OS versions)
> 4. Log of any selective wipe events in the audit period
> 5. Evidence of a blocked non-compliant device (conditional access sign-in log showing denial)
